extracted.intended_audience: policymakers, regulatory analysts, academics, media, and the public interested in federal regulatory policy
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for federal agencies on how to conduct economic analyses of proposed regulations, including how to value benefits and costs, account for distributional (equity) effects, incorporate behavioral economics, and set social discounting practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circular A-4 as primary guidance for economic analyses
rubrics_metrics.description: Circular A-4 is the primary guidance document on federal agencies’ economic analyses of regulations and determines how agencies estimate the costs and benefits of rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should follow Circular A-4 when conducting regulatory cost–benefit analysis; the document plays a key role in federal regulatory policy and modernization of analytical practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of benefits that occur in the future or outside the United States
rubrics_metrics.description: The updated guidance modernizes outdated practices including consideration of benefits that occur in the future or outside the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should include and properly value benefits that accrue in the distant future or to parties outside the U.S., reflecting contemporary evidence about how such benefits should be treated in regulatory analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment of equity concerns related to distribution of regulatory impacts
rubrics_metrics.description: The guidance calls for assessment of equity concerns related to the distribution of regulatory impacts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory analyses should evaluate distributional effects so policymakers understand who bears costs and who receives benefits; analyses should not ignore equity concerns and should inform fair policymaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incorporation of behavioral economics issues
rubrics_metrics.description: The updates modernize consideration of behavioral economics issues in regulatory analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyses should incorporate behavioral-economics insights (how people actually behave versus assumptions of perfect rationality) when estimating costs, benefits, and policy impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply a social discount rate of 2%
rubrics_metrics.description: The new guidance provides for a social discount rate of 2%.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although described as a conservative choice by some economic scholarship, adopting a 2% social discount rate is intended to better reflect current evidence compared with older, higher rates used since 2003 and to increase the present value of future benefits in analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Update the social discount rate every three years
rubrics_metrics.description: The guidance calls for updating the social discount rate every three years to capture new economic data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should periodically revise the discount rate (on a three-year schedule) to incorporate emerging economic evidence, ensuring analyses remain current and data-driven.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the latest scientific methods and best available information
rubrics_metrics.description: Efficient and effective government policy requires sound analysis grounded in the latest scientific methods; agencies should adapt to incorporate the best available information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory analysis should be evidence-based and reflect contemporary methodological advances so that policymaking is more rational, efficient, effective, and fair.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize greater valuation of distant-future benefits and costs
rubrics_metrics.description: Current economic evidence demonstrates that individuals place far greater value on benefits and costs accruing in the distant future than once believed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analysts should adjust valuation practices to reflect evidence that distant-future impacts matter more to people than older guidelines assumed, which bears on discounting and benefit–cost calculations.
